content_metadata.description: This video presents a scientific research project on producing activated carbon from soybean waste and testing its ability to capture the fungicide chlorothalonil.

qAndA.answer: Soybean paste, a residue left over from soybean oil production.
qAndA.question: What is the specific agroindustrial waste used in this research?
What is the particle size of the soybean paste used in the static pyrolysis reactions?
What is the name of the chemical used to analyze the gas products after the static pyrolysis reaction?
What solvents were used in the Soxhlet apparatus to wash the carbon?

qAndA.answer: The carbon from soybean waste demonstrated significant retention ability, decreasing the signal of chlorothalonil by over 70%, but the commercial activated carbon achieved 100% retention.

youtube_description: Soybean residues were transformed through static pyrolysis carried out at temperatures between 250 °C and 350  °C. The gaseous fraction analysis showed that the gases emanated in the pyrolysis are mainly CO2 and CO. Furthermore, it was proved that this methodology constitutes a simple way to obtain useful carbons for the capture of pesticides present in an aqueous matrix. For example, the concentration of Chlorothalonil in a 7:3 water: acetonitrile solution decreases by 76-77 % through adsorption on the carbons obtained.
youtube_title: PYROLYSIS OF SOYBEAN WASTE: A ROUTE TO ACTIVATED CARBON FOR FUNGICIDE CHLOROTHALONIL CAPTURE
